title: Handling automations on 2D sprites with customizable gear
author: operatingcan
selftext:
I have been working on this Maple Story-style game. The biggest challenge I've run into so far is getting consistent animations and clean frames for frame-based animations of a 2D character where you can mix and match gear. I thought this would be a nice opportunity to share progress as well as talk about methodology. 

  
Methodology is basically 2 parts here:  
\- Layering gear, cropping hair, etc concerns  
\- Generating all animation frames for a given piece of gear

For layering I've set up a (surely overly rudimentary) layering order per frame. That way we can have an arm in front of torso in frame 2 but behind in frame 3, etc. Some peices of clothing are also broken into separate layers for things like shoulders/arms parts of shirts.

https://reddit.com/link/1xsw9cc/video/mmbok9c77u0i1/player

Hair cropping is currently being done with a mask that essentially cuts all hair off and is drawn per piece of gear, by AI, but after all of the image gen etc. I occasionally have to yap at it but it works decently. However it falls quite flat on things like bandana gear where some hair on top should appear but not all, etc. I want to avoid having to redraw every hairstyle for every hat "type" but I think that's the best solution long term at least for some hat types.

As for generating all the frames, the only workflow that finally gave me satisfactory results is:

1. An artist hand-draws every frame for 1 body/outfit  
2. I feed those, layer by layer, into AI. I've done a few masks but generally one overall image, one where all right limbs are colored red and all left limbs blue etc, and then the specific piece of gear (and just the frame of that piece) and then I ask it first to generate an overall concept image and then generate each layer, following the same sillhouette as the hand drawn one. It can add a bit extra but generally needs to follow that same sillhouette.  
3. A bunch of your normal post-processing checks, re-generations, etc until it looks good.

Although hats and shirts are the most complicated, my character's head doesn't turn as part of the animations so I've been able to have a variety of hats without an artist hand drawing each sillhouette, which helps a lot with the outfits feeling like they have diversity even if the sillhouettes are a fairly restricted set for now.

I banged my head on this for \~12hrs across a few days but could not get anything that could understand what the anatomy was doing in 2D, so given frames would be all skewompous or just janked up. Ironically I've had an easier time getting claude/codex to do skeletal animations of 3d rigs via blender etc. than these 2d rigs. My best solution was a 3d rig and then convert "views" of that, but it still ended up looking bad mostly due to my lack of artistic ability.

Having an artist still hand-draw each animation frame is mind-numbing work for them and a real drag for making equips that work across all classes etc. I'm hoping that with a larger corpus of "approved" gear and animations I might be able to start getting better results without an artist involved for every piece of gear. We'll see.

Also I tried using krita for manually editing images via MCP or computer control, it never could produce very good results -- felt a bit like it was trying things blind without a good way to "see" its work and course correct. Very similar to how using blender via computer control felt, but the MCP fixed that with blender's case. Hoping that eventually I'll either stumble on a tool that does that better, or krita MCP improves, but for now been sticking with a lot more image gen and a lot less draw-tool tweaking of existing images. 

Attached is a short gameplay teaser that shows some of this work off along with a few screencaps showing frame by frame and methodology a bit. Cheers, hope this helps someone.

comments.author: AstrialWorldDev
comments.body:
This is a really useful breakdown, thanks for sharing! I hadn’t thought about AI struggling with anatomy in 2D rather than just the image generation itself. Colouring the left and right limbs differently in the reference images is a pretty clever workaround.

I’m curious about one thing though. Since the head doesn’t turn in the animations, do you think the same approach would work with different camera angles, or would you need an artist to redraw those frames?

Good luck with the gear system too, sounds like a lot of work!

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: It may help to lock down a small sprite-sheet contract before expanding the gear set: fixed canvas and pivot, named pose/frame IDs, and explicit front/back masks for each frame. Keep one golden base animation as a transparent overlay target so shifts in silhouette or alignment show up before importing a whole batch. Then test one difficult hat and one layered shirt across every pose, since those edge cases will tell you whether the mask setup scales. That separates generation drift from a one-off cleanup issue.
